client: I just feel so overwhelmed by all these medical bills piling up after my surgery. Every time I think I've got a handle on it, another bill shows up, and it sends me into this spiral of anxiety about how I'm going to pay for everything. I know therapy is supposed to help, but I'm not sure how talking about it will make the bills go away.
therapist: It sounds like this situation is weighing heavily on you, and that constant stream of bills keeps pulling you back into that anxious spiral. While talking won’t make the bills disappear, we can work on how these thoughts are affecting you—would you be open to exploring what goes through your mind when a new bill arrives?

client:
Yeah, I guess I could try talking about that. When I see a new bill in the mail, my chest just tightens up immediately. I start thinking "I'll never get ahead" and then my mind races to all the other bills still unpaid—it's like a domino effect of panic. 

I don't know if talking will help though, because the problem is real—I actually don't have enough money. It's not just in my head.
therapist: Your anxiety makes complete sense—these are real financial pressures, and your body is reacting to that very real stress. What I hear you saying is that while the problem is real, the way your thoughts escalate ("I'll never get ahead") adds another layer of distress—would it help to look at how those thoughts might be making the situation feel even heavier?

client: I get what you're saying about my thoughts making it worse, but it's hard not to spiral when I look at my bank account. The numbers don't lie - I really am falling further behind every month. When I try to think positively, it just feels like I'm lying to myself.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two painful extremes—either spiraling into despair or feeling like you're forcing false positivity. That middle ground is where we can work: instead of "positive thinking," could we explore small ways to approach this situation that feel honest but don't amplify the overwhelm?

client: I like the idea of finding a middle ground, but I'm not sure how to do that when my brain automatically jumps to worst-case scenarios. Even when I try to be neutral, it feels like I'm just pretending not to be anxious. How do you make that shift feel genuine?
therapist: It sounds like you're wrestling with two very human things right now—the real weight of your situation, and your mind's natural tendency to protect you by anticipating the worst. Rather than forcing a shift, what if we honored that protective instinct while gently asking, "What's one small piece of this that feels manageable to look at today?" Would that seem more genuine than trying to overhaul your thinking all at once?

client:
I appreciate you acknowledging that my mind is trying to protect me, but when you ask about finding a manageable piece to look at... I don't know, everything feels tangled together right now. The anxiety about work, the loneliness at night - it all feeds into each other and picking one piece feels impossible. 

I guess what I'm saying is that even the idea of breaking it down makes me feel overwhelmed because I worry I'll just spiral back to the big picture anyway. Does that make sense?
therapist:
It makes complete sense—when everything feels so tightly knotted together, trying to pull one thread can make the whole bundle seem even more tangled. That fear of spiraling back is your mind trying to protect you from getting overwhelmed, even while the overwhelm is already here. 

Rather than forcing you to pick a thread, would it help if we just sat with how exhausting it feels to carry all these worries at once? Sometimes naming the weight can make it feel a little less crushing.

client:
Honestly, sitting with the exhaustion sounds both relieving and terrifying at the same time. Part of me wants to just collapse under the weight of it all, but another part is scared that if I really acknowledge how heavy this feels, I'll completely fall apart. 

I do appreciate you not pushing me to "fix" things right away though. It's just... when I've tried naming these feelings before, they've swallowed me whole. How do you stay with something that painful without getting completely lost in it?
therapist:
It sounds like you're bravely facing this impossible choice—between the relief of acknowledging your exhaustion and the fear of being overwhelmed by it. That tension itself is exhausting to hold. 

What if we tried something small—not diving into the feelings, but just noticing together when they start to feel "too big"? Like watching the tide come in while standing safely on shore? Would that gentle approach feel more manageable right now?

client: I like the idea of watching from the shore, but I'm not sure I can stop myself from getting pulled under. When the feelings come, they don't feel like a tide—more like getting hit by a wave out of nowhere. How am I supposed to just notice when everything feels urgent?
therapist:
It makes sense that these feelings don't feel gradual like a tide—when they hit, it's sudden and all-consuming, making it hard to step back. That urgency is real, and trying to "just notice" might feel impossible when you're already in the wave. 

What if we started even smaller—not during the wave itself, but in the quieter moments after? Could we explore what helps you catch your breath when the worst of it passes?

client: I guess I do have moments where the anxiety eases up a bit, but even then I'm just waiting for the next wave to hit. It's like I can't fully relax because I know the bad feelings will come back. And when you say "catch my breath," I don't even know what that would look like—everything just feels exhausting.
therapist:
It sounds like even the brief respites from anxiety get overshadowed by anticipation of the next difficult wave—that constant vigilance must be so draining. When everything feels exhausting, even small acts of rest can feel out of reach. 

Could we explore what "catching your breath" might look like in your daily life—not as something big, but perhaps noticing when your shoulders relax for just a moment, or when you take one deeper breath without realizing it? Those tiny moments might be more accessible than we think.

client:
I get what you're saying about small moments, but when I do notice my shoulders relaxing or take a deep breath, my brain immediately jumps to "this won't last" and the anxiety comes rushing back. It's like my body gets these tiny breaks but my mind won't let me enjoy them. 

I've tried mindfulness apps before and they just made me more frustrated because I couldn't stop analyzing whether I was doing it "right." How is noticing these moments supposed to help when they disappear so fast?
therapist:
It sounds like your mind is quick to interrupt even the smallest moments of relief with warnings—almost as if relaxing feels unsafe somehow. That automatic "this won't last" thought is understandable when you've been carrying so much for so long. 

Rather than aiming to "enjoy" these moments (which can feel like pressure), what if we simply acknowledged how hard it is to trust respite when it comes? The noticing itself—even when brief—might still matter. Does that shift feel any different to you?

client:
I get what you're saying about just noticing instead of forcing enjoyment, but it's frustrating because even when I try that, my brain just keeps screaming "danger!" in the background. It's like I can't even pause long enough to acknowledge the moment before the anxiety crashes back in. 

The idea that noticing matters feels too small, honestly. When I'm in that panicked state, it's hard to believe something so subtle could make any difference.
therapist:
It sounds like that "danger" signal is so loud right now that even small steps forward feel frustratingly insignificant—and that frustration makes complete sense when you're in the thick of it. The fact that you're still trying despite that is actually meaningful, even if it doesn't feel that way yet. 

Could we slow down and explore what happens if, instead of fighting that "danger" signal, we simply acknowledge it's there? Not to change it, but to understand why it's working so hard to protect you?
